newsitem.title: USA: Anti-smoking supporters doubtful over global pact.
newsitem.headline: Anti-smoking supporters doubtful over global pact.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Several leading anti-smoking proponents said Thursday they were pessimistic that a global settlement can ultimately be reached with the tobacco industry, but predicted manufacturers may initiate efforts in the next few months.

Although speculation has been mounting that the industry would eventually end litigation through a legislative settlement, panellists discussing the topic at American University's Washington College of Law said they doubted all the diverse parties could ever reach an agreement.

But they said next week's beginning of a personal injury trial by the lawyer who won a verdict against the industry last summer, along with the summer trial of the first Medicaid suit brought by a state attorney general will motivate the tobacco industry to take some action, possibly approaching Congress in the next few months.
"I think they will make a run at it," said James Tierney, a former Maine attorney general who is coordinating Medicaid litigation brought by 22 states.
"I think something is going to happen. Do we really think the tobacco industry is just going to roll the dice before a chancery judge in Mississippi?" he said.
The Mississippi case is scheduled to go to trial in July. Mississippi was the first of 22 states to sue the industry to recoup health care costs of smokers.

Jury selection is also scheduled to begin Monday in Florida in Connor vs RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co. Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.. The plaintiffs lawyer is Norwood "Woody" Wilner, who won a $750,000 verdict last summer against Brown & Williamson, a unit of B.A.T Industries.
The verdict toppled tobacco stocks and resulted in hundreds of more lawsuits against the industry.

Tierney said he believed that the fact that the tobacco industry has recently hired two politically well-connected Washington law firms is evidence that they plan to approach members of Congress soon.
However, he said it would be difficult to reach an agreement that would satisfy all parties.

The attorneys general alone have developed a statement of goals that include full disclosure of the health effects of tobacco products, the creation of a large pool of funds to pay for health care of smokers, reduction of access of children and reforming tobacco companies' business practices.
Despite the difficulties of an accord, panellists said the industry is coming under increasing pressure to find a solution to mounting litigation and other attacks.

Not only are a number of Medicaid, individual and class action suits scheduled to begin this year, but the proceedings will receive a boost from Liggett Group's historic settlement with state attorneys general in which it admitted that nicotine is addictive and agreed to turn over internal documents.

If judges presiding over the 22 state suits determine the sensitive papers can be used as evidence, the documents could prove damaging to the industry not just in the Medicaid cases but in other trials as well. Liggett is owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd.

In addition, a North Carolina federal judge is expected to rule soon on the industry's challenge to Food and Drug Administration regulation of tobacco sales and marketing. The Justice Department is also conducting a criminal investigation of the industry concerning allegations that it withheld health information from government agencies.
"Never before has the tobacco industry faced such a period of uncertainty and vulnerability," said Matthew Myers, general counsel of the National Centre on Tobacco-Free Kids.
While he expressed doubts about a possible global settlement, he added, "If it's ever going to happen, I think it will happen in the next 12 months."
But he went on to caution that the tobacco industry's history "does not give rise to optimism."
Mary Aronson, a public policy analyst for institutional investors, said she thought a global settlement is the only answer for the manufacturers.
"If the industry is to remain in business ... the only way that can happen and the industry can find peace is through a legislative settlement."
